questions.q: The word 'deepfake' blends 'fake' with which other term?
questions.fact: Many are made by two neural networks trained against each other — one inventing images, the other trying to spot the fakes.
questions.q_fr: Le mot « deepfake » associe « fake » (faux) à quel autre terme ?
questions.fact_fr: Beaucoup sont produits par deux réseaux de neurones qui s'affrontent : l'un fabrique des images, l'autre tente de repérer les fausses.

questions.why: Answer correct — the cited article defines a patch as data 'often to fix bugs and security vulnerabilities'. The etymology in the fact is near-verbatim from the article: suppliers expected 'the recipient to cut out the indicated part of the original tape (or deck), and patch in (hence the name) the replacement segment'. French renders 'patch' as 'rustine', which is the right idiom.
questions.q: Why does a software update often matter for your safety, not just for new features?
options: It makes the battery last longer
It deletes old files to free up space
It closes security holes attackers already know
questions.fact: The English word 'patch' is literal: suppliers once posted punched tape, and you cut out the faulty stretch and spliced the fix in.
questions.q_fr: Pourquoi une mise à jour logicielle concerne-t-elle souvent votre sécurité, et pas seulement les nouveautés ?
options_fr: Elle allonge l'autonomie de la batterie
Elle supprime les vieux fichiers pour libérer de la place
Elle bouche des failles que les attaquants connaissent déjà
Elle change votre mot de passe automatiquement
questions.fact_fr: Le mot anglais « patch » (rustine) est littéral : on recevait une bande perforée, on découpait le passage fautif et on y raccordait le morceau corrigé.

questions.why: Answer correct. Both statistics verified verbatim in the cited article: '81% of users have reused a password across two or more sites' and credential stuffing achieving 'up to a 2% login success rate'. The fact attributes the figure to a survey rather than stating it as universal — correctly hedged. Distractors are same-kind wrong mechanisms.
questions.q: A shopping site you use suffers a data breach. Why does that put your other accounts at risk?
options: The breach spreads through your Wi-Fi
Attackers try the same email and password elsewhere
Your bank uses the same servers
questions.fact: One survey found 81% of people reuse a password on two or more sites; attackers automate the retries and up to 2% succeed.
questions.q_fr: Un site marchand que vous utilisez subit une fuite de données. Pourquoi vos autres comptes sont-ils en danger ?
options_fr: La fuite se propage par votre Wi-Fi
Des attaquants essaient le même couple adresse-mot de passe ailleurs
Votre banque utilise les mêmes serveurs
Votre numéro de téléphone change automatiquement
questions.fact_fr: Une enquête a trouvé que 81 % des gens réutilisent un mot de passe sur au moins deux sites ; jusqu'à 2 % des essais automatisés réussissent.

questions.why: Answer correct: the defining property of E2EE is that the intermediary holds no key. Distractors 0-2 are exactly the parties E2EE is designed to exclude, so there is no second right answer. The fact does not restate the question — it explains the mechanism. kids:false and diff 3 are the right calls; the honest caveats (metadata, compromised endpoints, cloud backups) sit outside the narrow claim 'read your message'.
questions.q: In an end-to-end encrypted chat, who else can read your message besides you and the person you sent it to?
options: Nobody, not even the company running the app
questions.fact: The message is scrambled on your device and unscrambled on theirs; the service carries a package it holds no key to.
questions.q_fr: Dans une messagerie chiffrée de bout en bout, qui peut lire votre message à part vous et votre destinataire ?
options_fr: N'importe qui sur le même Wi-Fi
Personne, pas même l'entreprise qui édite l'application
questions.fact_fr: Le message est chiffré sur votre appareil et déchiffré sur le sien : le service transporte un colis dont il n'a pas la clé.

questions.why: Wikipedia Rainbow: 'In a primary rainbow, the arc shows red on the outer part and violet on the inner side.' Newton's five-then-seven colours and the musical-scale analogy confirmed verbatim in the same article. Distractors are all real spectrum colours, all unambiguously not outermost. French idiomatic, same order.
questions.q: In a rainbow, which colour sits on the outer edge of the arc?
questions.fact: Newton first counted five colours, then added orange and indigo to make seven — matching the notes of a musical scale.
questions.q_fr: Dans un arc-en-ciel, quelle couleur se trouve sur le bord extérieur de l'arc ?
questions.fact_fr: Newton comptait d'abord cinq couleurs, puis ajouta l'orange et l'indigo pour en avoir sept, comme les notes d'une gamme.

questions.why: RGB additive model correct; RGB_color_model is a real article about the subject. Distractor 1 (CMY) is the subtractive set and distractor 0 (RYB) the artists' set — plausible, same kind, both unambiguously wrong for emitted light. Fact is checkable and not a restatement.
questions.q: A television or phone screen builds every colour it shows by mixing just three colours of light. Which three?
questions.fact: Hold a magnifier to a white patch of screen and there is no white there at all — only tiny red, green and blue dots.
questions.q_fr: Un écran de télévision ou de téléphone fabrique toutes ses couleurs en mélangeant seulement trois couleurs de lumière. Lesquelles ?
questions.fact_fr: Regardez une zone blanche de l'écran à la loupe : il n'y a aucun blanc, seulement de minuscules points rouges, verts et bleus.

questions.why: Inferior mirage: light from the sky is refracted upward by the hot low-density air layer, so the 'puddle' is displaced sky. Correct. Distractor 1 ('illusion inside your eye') is the common misconception and is directly refuted by the fact. src Mirage is the subject article. French correct.
questions.q: On a hot road a shimmering 'puddle' appears ahead, then vanishes as you get closer. What are you actually seeing?
options: Water evaporating off the warm tarmac
An illusion created inside your own eye
Heat glowing upward from the road surface
A patch of sky, bent upwards by hot air
questions.fact: A mirage is not in your head — a camera photographs it too, because the light really is being bent.
questions.q_fr: Sur une route chaude, une « flaque » scintillante apparaît au loin puis disparaît quand on s'approche. Que voit-on en réalité ?
options_fr: De l'eau qui s'évapore du bitume chaud
Une illusion créée à l'intérieur de l'œil
La chaleur qui rayonne depuis la chaussée
Un morceau de ciel, dévié vers le haut par l'air chaud
questions.fact_fr: Un mirage n'est pas dans la tête : un appareil photo le capte aussi, car la lumière est réellement déviée.

questions.why: Wikipedia Ibn al-Haytham: 'the first to correctly prove vision as intromissive rather than extramissive'; Book of Optics written 1011–1021 in Cairo (1015 sits inside that window); 'Legend has it that Alhazen feigned madness and was kept under house arrest during this period. During this time, he wrote his influential Book of Optics.' Fact correctly flags it as legend. Distractor 0 is the Greek emission theory he refuted — plausible, same kind, wrong.
questions.q: Around 1015, working in Cairo, the scholar Ibn al-Haytham showed that we see because:
options: the eye sends out rays that touch objects
light travels from objects into the eye
the air carries images along to the eye
the mind projects pictures onto the world
questions.fact: He set out the argument in a seven-volume Book of Optics, written by legend while he was confined after feigning madness.
questions.q_fr: Vers 1015, au Caire, le savant Ibn al-Haytham démontra que nous voyons parce que :
options_fr: l'œil émet des rayons qui touchent les objets
la lumière va des objets jusqu'à l'œil
l'air transporte les images jusqu'à l'œil
l'esprit projette des images sur le monde
questions.fact_fr: Il l'expose dans un Traité d'optique en sept volumes, écrit selon la légende alors qu'il était reclus après avoir simulé la folie.

questions.why: Correct: finite speed of light, 1676. The derived figure (~220,000 km/s via Huygens) is about 26% below the true value, so 'about a quarter too low' is accurate. src is the dedicated article on exactly this determination. Distractor 0 fails because Jupiter's four Galilean moons were known from 1610 — plausible-sounding but clearly not what the timings showed.
questions.q: In 1676 Ole Rømer timed the eclipses of Io, a moon of Jupiter. What did his timings prove?
options: That Jupiter has more than one moon
That light is bent as it passes planets
That light travels at a finite speed
That Jupiter's orbit is not circular
questions.fact: His figure came out about a quarter too low, but it was the first proof that light takes time to cross space.
questions.q_fr: En 1676, Ole Rømer chronométra les éclipses d'Io, une lune de Jupiter. Que prouvèrent ses mesures ?
options_fr: Que la lumière est déviée près des planètes
Que la lumière a une vitesse finie
Que l'orbite de Jupiter n'est pas circulaire
questions.fact_fr: Sa valeur était inférieure d'environ un quart à la réalité, mais c'était la première preuve que la lumière met du temps à voyager.

questions.why: Doppler effect, correctly described as compression ahead and stretching behind. Distractor 2 ('sound travels faster towards a listener') is the classic wrong intuition and is genuinely false — the wave speed is set by the medium. Doppler weather radar payoff is accurate and in the cited article. French idiomatic.
questions.q: Why does an ambulance siren sound higher as it comes towards you and lower once it has passed?
options: The sound waves bunch up ahead of it and stretch out behind
The driver switches the siren to a different setting
Sound travels faster when it is heading towards a listener
Your ears gradually adjust to the very loud noise
questions.fact: Weather radar uses the same shift: the returning signal shows which way rain inside a storm is moving.
questions.q_fr: Pourquoi la sirène d'une ambulance semble-t-elle plus aiguë quand elle approche, puis plus grave une fois passée ?
options_fr: Les ondes sonores se resserrent devant elle et s'étirent derrière
Le conducteur change le réglage de la sirène
Le son va plus vite lorsqu'il se dirige vers l'auditeur
L'oreille s'adapte peu à peu au bruit très fort
questions.fact_fr: Les radars météo exploitent le même décalage : le signal renvoyé révèle dans quel sens la pluie se déplace dans un orage.

questions.why: Correct: coalesced pressure waves form a shock cone whose intersection with the ground is the boom carpet. The fact directly kills the 'one bang at the moment of breaking through' myth and matches the cited article's boom-carpet section. Distractor 2 ('a solid barrier being broken') is the misconception the phrase 'sound barrier' creates — plausible, unambiguously wrong.
questions.q: What produces the sonic boom heard when an aircraft flies faster than sound?
options: The engines backfiring as the aircraft passes the speed of sound
Pressure waves piling into a shock wave that sweeps over the ground
A solid barrier in the air being physically broken apart
Air freezing and then shattering in the wake of the wings
questions.fact: The boom is not a single bang at the moment of breaking through — it trails the aircraft like a wake, all along its path.
questions.q_fr: Qu'est-ce qui produit le bang supersonique entendu quand un avion vole plus vite que le son ?
options_fr: Les moteurs qui pétaradent au passage de la vitesse du son
Des ondes de pression accumulées en onde de choc qui balaie le sol
Une barrière solide dans l'air qui se brise physiquement
L'air qui gèle puis se fracture dans le sillage des ailes
questions.fact_fr: Le bang n'est pas un claquement unique au passage du mur du son : il suit l'avion comme un sillage, tout au long de sa trajectoire.

questions.why: Answer and distractors are sound. But the fact claimed 'Skin cannot measure temperature at all' — an absolute that overstates the physiology and is not supported by the cited Thermal_conduction article. Softened to 'does not sense temperature, only heat flowing in or out', which is the standard and defensible formulation. French adjusted to match.
questions.q: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have sat in the same room all night. Why does the metal one feel colder?
options: The metal really is at a lower temperature
Wood quietly gives off a little heat of its own
Metal carries heat away from your hand much faster
Metal reflects your body heat straight back at you
questions.fact: Skin does not sense temperature, only heat flowing in or out — so good conductors always feel cold.
questions.q_fr: Une cuillère en métal et une cuillère en bois ont passé la nuit dans la même pièce. Pourquoi le métal semble-t-il plus froid ?
options_fr: Le métal est réellement à une température plus basse
Le bois dégage discrètement un peu de chaleur
Le métal évacue la chaleur de la main bien plus vite
Le métal renvoie la chaleur du corps vers la main
questions.fact_fr: La peau ne mesure pas la température mais la chaleur qui entre ou qui sort : les bons conducteurs paraissent donc toujours froids.

questions.why: Wikipedia C. V. Raman confirms all three load-bearing claims: 1930 Nobel for the scattering of light and the effect named after him; 'the first Asian and non-White person to receive a Nobel Prize in Physics'; and the September 1921 voyage on which he 'contemplated the blue color of the Mediterranean Sea'. Distractors are real optical phenomena (birefringence, Faraday effect) that are not Raman scattering. French correct.
questions.q: The Indian physicist C. V. Raman won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics for showing that light passing through a material can do what?
options: Split into two beams of equal brightness
questions.fact: He was the first Asian to win the physics Nobel, and it began with a question: why is the Mediterranean so blue?
questions.q_fr: Le physicien indien C. V. Raman reçut le prix Nobel de physique 1930 pour avoir montré que la lumière traversant un matériau peut :
options_fr: se diviser en deux faisceaux d'égale intensité
questions.fact_fr: Il fut le premier Asiatique à recevoir le Nobel de physique ; tout est parti d'une question : pourquoi la Méditerranée est-elle si bleue ?

questions.why: Faraday's 1831 discovery, correctly stated. Strictly an EMF is induced and current flows only in a closed circuit, but the cited article's canonical experiment is a coil on a galvanometer, so the phrasing is fair for a quiz. Distractors are plausible novice guesses, none defensible. Power-station payoff accurate.
questions.q: What happens when a magnet is moved in and out of a coil of wire?
options: The wire heats up and nothing more
An electric current flows in the wire
questions.fact: Michael Faraday found this in 1831; nearly every power station still makes electricity by spinning magnets past coils.
questions.q_fr: Que se passe-t-il lorsqu'on fait entrer et sortir un aimant d'une bobine de fil ?
options_fr: Le fil chauffe, et rien de plus
Il ne se passe absolument rien
Un courant électrique circule dans le fil
questions.fact_fr: Michael Faraday le découvrit en 1831 ; presque toutes les centrales produisent encore l'électricité en faisant tourner des aimants devant des bobines.

questions.why: Question and answer verified verbatim against Voltaic_pile ('stacked several pairs of alternating copper (or silver) and zinc discs separated by cloth or cardboard soaked in brine'; 'first electrical battery'). But the fact said 'within weeks' — the cited article dates Nicholson and Carlisle's electrolysis of water only to 1800, with no interval given. Tightened to 'the same year', which the article does support. French updated.
questions.q: In 1800 Alessandro Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper separated by brine-soaked cloth. What had he built?
questions.fact: Until then electricity came only in sudden sparks; the same year, chemists used Volta's steady current to split water.
questions.q_fr: En 1800, Alessandro Volta empila des disques de zinc et de cuivre séparés par des tissus imbibés de saumure. Qu'avait-il construit ?
questions.fact_fr: Jusque-là l'électricité n'existait qu'en étincelles ; dès la même année, des chimistes utilisaient son courant continu pour décomposer l'eau.

questions.why: Answer correct — Wikipedia Compass: 2nd-century-BC 'Chinese geomancers were experimenting with the magnetic properties of lodestone to make a south-pointing spoon for divination'; navigation only 'by 1088 during the Song dynasty, as described by Shen Kuo'. But the fact asserted flatly that Han diviners USED such a spoon, while the same article says 'archaeologists have yet to discover an actual spoon made of magnetite in a Han tomb'. Rewritten around that non-discovery, which is both accurate and a stronger payoff. French rewritten to match.
questions.q: The magnetic compass was invented in China. What was it first used for?
questions.fact: Archaeologists have never actually dug up one of the famous lodestone spoons; compasses only began steering ships around 1088.
questions.q_fr: La boussole magnétique fut inventée en Chine. À quoi servait-elle d'abord ?
options_fr: À diriger les navires en pleine mer
À la divination et à l'orientation des bâtiments
À repérer les minerais dans le sol
questions.fact_fr: Aucune des fameuses cuillères en magnétite n'a jamais été retrouvée par les archéologues ; la boussole ne guide les navires que vers 1088.

questions.why: Apollo 15, 2 August 1971, David Scott's televised hammer-and-feather drop; the feather came from the Air Force Academy's falcon and the lunar module was named Falcon. Both hit the surface together. src Apollo_15 covers the demonstration. Fact adds the Galileo link without restating the question. French correct, same order.
questions.q: On the Moon in 1971, astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather at the same moment. What happened?
options: The feather reached the ground first
The hammer landed well before the feather
questions.fact: With no air to slow the feather, gravity pulls everything down at the same rate — Galileo's claim, tested live on television.
questions.q_fr: Sur la Lune en 1971, l'astronaute David Scott lâcha en même temps un marteau et une plume de faucon. Que s'est-il passé ?
options_fr: La plume a touché le sol la première
Le marteau est arrivé bien avant la plume
Ils ont touché le sol ensemble
La plume s'est envolée sur le côté
questions.fact_fr: Sans air pour freiner la plume, la gravité accélère tout de la même façon : l'affirmation de Galilée, vérifiée en direct à la télévision.

questions.why: Checked the 'thirty horses' figure, which was the main risk. Wikipedia Magdeburg_hemispheres: 'performed on 8 May 1654 in front of the Imperial Diet, and the Emperor Ferdinand III in Regensburg. Thirty horses, in two teams of fifteen, could not separate the hemispheres until the valve was opened.' Date, horse count, two teams and the valve detail all confirmed. Hemispheres were copper, so 'metal' is accurate. Distractors same-kind and wrong.
questions.q: In 1654 Otto von Guericke pumped the air out of two metal hemispheres pressed together. What could two teams of horses not do?
options: Lift them clear off the ground
questions.fact: Thirty horses failed, yet only the weight of the outside air held the halves together — open a valve and they came apart by hand.
questions.q_fr: En 1654, Otto von Guericke fit le vide dans deux hémisphères métalliques accolés. Que deux attelages de chevaux n'ont-ils pas réussi à faire ?
options_fr: Les faire rouler sur la place
questions.fact_fr: Trente chevaux ont échoué, alors que seul le poids de l'air extérieur maintenait les moitiés : en ouvrant une valve, on les séparait à la main.

questions.why: Archimedes' principle correctly stated. Distractor 2 is quantitatively false (steel ~7.8 vs seawater ~1.03 g/cm3) so there is no reading where two options are right. Archimedes lived c. 287–212 BCE, so 'over 2,200 years ago' is safe. French uses the correct '2 200' convention and preserves option order.
questions.q: Why does a steel ship float when a steel nail sinks?
options: Steel behaves as a lighter material in very large pieces
The hull pushes aside a weight of water equal to the whole ship
Seawater is denser than the steel the hull is made of
The ship's engines constantly push it upwards in the water
questions.fact: Archimedes set it out over 2,200 years ago: the upward push equals the weight of the fluid the object shoves aside.
questions.q_fr: Pourquoi un navire en acier flotte-t-il alors qu'un clou en acier coule ?
options_fr: L'acier devient plus léger lorsqu'il est en très grosses pièces
La coque déplace un poids d'eau égal à celui du navire entier
L'eau de mer est plus dense que l'acier de la coque
Les moteurs du navire le poussent en permanence vers le haut
questions.fact_fr: Archimède l'a énoncé il y a plus de 2 200 ans : la poussée vers le haut égale le poids du fluide déplacé par l'objet.

questions.why: Answer confirmed: the cited article states 'Einstein was awarded the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.' But the fact ended 'it is how solar cells work' — the same article opens with the hatnote 'Not to be confused with Photovoltaic effect' and treats photovoltaics as a separate phenomenon. That claim is unsupported by the source and conflates two effects, so I replaced it with the threshold-frequency result, which is the actual quantum clue and is squarely in the article. French rewritten.
questions.q: Albert Einstein's Nobel Prize in Physics was not awarded for relativity. What was it awarded for?
options: Predicting the existence of black holes
questions.fact: No matter how bright a red light is, it knocks no electrons out of some metals — the clue that told Einstein light comes in packets.
questions.q_fr: Le prix Nobel de physique d'Albert Einstein ne récompense pas la relativité. Que récompense-t-il ?
options_fr: La prédiction de l'existence des trous noirs
questions.fact_fr: Une lumière rouge, si intense soit-elle, n'arrache aucun électron à certains métaux : l'indice qui révéla à Einstein que la lumière arrive par paquets.

questions.why: Historical error in the stem. The cited article says 'This type of experiment was first DESCRIBED by Thomas Young in 1801', that his 1803 demonstrations used 'sunlight, pinholes and cards', and explicitly that 'there is some question as to whether he ever actually performed a double-slit interference experiment'. Asserting he shone light through two slits in 1801 is not supportable. Stem changed to 'described sending light through', tense moved to the present for the result. Answer, distractors and the one-particle-at-a-time payoff all stand. French updated in parallel.
questions.q: In 1801 Thomas Young described sending light through two narrow slits side by side. What appears on the screen behind them?
options: A pattern of bright and dark bands
questions.fact: The bands come from waves cancelling and reinforcing, and the pattern still builds up when particles are sent one at a time.
questions.q_fr: En 1801, Thomas Young décrivit le passage de la lumière par deux fentes étroites côte à côte. Qu'apparaît-il sur l'écran derrière ?
options_fr: Une alternance de bandes claires et sombres
questions.fact_fr: Ces bandes viennent d'ondes qui s'annulent ou s'additionnent, et la figure se forme même en envoyant les particules une par une.

questions.why: Hafele and Keating, 1971, commercial flights, caesium beam clocks. The measured results in the fact match the published values exactly: eastward −59 ns, westward +273 ns, against predictions of −40±23 and +275±21. 'Close to relativity's prediction' is appropriately hedged rather than overstated. src is the dedicated article. French numerals and phrasing correct.
questions.q: In 1971 two researchers flew caesium atomic clocks around the world on ordinary passenger flights. What did they find on landing?
options: Every clock had stayed perfectly in step
The clocks had stopped while at high altitude
The travelling clocks disagreed with the clocks left behind
The clocks ran fast only while over the poles
questions.fact: Flying east the clocks lost about 59 billionths of a second; flying west they gained about 273 — close to relativity's prediction.
questions.q_fr: En 1971, deux chercheurs firent voyager des horloges atomiques au césium autour du monde sur des vols de ligne. Qu'ont-ils constaté à l'arrivée ?
options_fr: Toutes les horloges étaient restées parfaitement synchrones
Les horloges s'étaient arrêtées en haute altitude
Les horloges voyageuses ne concordaient plus avec celles restées au sol
Les horloges n'avançaient qu'au-dessus des pôles
questions.fact_fr: Vers l'est elles ont perdu environ 59 milliardièmes de seconde, vers l'ouest elles en ont gagné environ 273 : proche de la prédiction relativiste.

questions.why: Fetched Eddington_experiment — real article, exists, and confirms the 29 May 1919 eclipse, the Sobral (Brazil) and Príncipe expeditions, the test of gravitational deflection of starlight, Einstein's 1.75 arcsec prediction being 'precisely twice the Newtonian value of 0.83 arcseconds', and that the November 1919 results marked 'the beginning of his international celebrity status'. Every clause of the fact checks out. Distractors same-kind astronomical propositions, all wrong.
questions.q: During the total solar eclipse of 29 May 1919, teams in Brazil and on the island of Príncipe photographed stars close to the Sun. What were they testing?
options: Whether the Sun has a solid surface
Whether light has a top speed
Whether the Moon has an atmosphere
questions.fact: The stars appeared shifted by roughly the amount Einstein predicted, twice Newton's figure, and he was world-famous overnight.
questions.q_fr: Lors de l'éclipse totale de Soleil du 29 mai 1919, des équipes au Brésil et sur l'île de Príncipe photographièrent des étoiles proches du Soleil. Que testaient-elles ?
options_fr: Si le Soleil possède une surface solide
Si la gravité dévie la lumière des étoiles
Si la lumière a une vitesse maximale
Si la Lune possède une atmosphère
questions.fact_fr: Les étoiles semblaient décalées d'à peu près ce qu'avait prédit Einstein, le double de la valeur newtonienne : il devint célèbre du jour au lendemain.

questions.why: Correct: mercury's resistance vanished at 4.2 K, Leiden, 1911. Persistent currents in superconducting loops with no measurable decay are documented in the cited article. Distractors are same-kind resistance behaviours (a rising resistance on cooling was in fact one of the rival predictions of the day, which makes option 1 genuinely plausible rather than filler). French uses '4,2' correctly.
questions.q: In 1911 Heike Kamerlingh Onnes cooled mercury to 4.2 degrees above absolute zero. What happened to its electrical resistance?
questions.fact: A current started in a superconducting loop keeps circulating with no battery and no measurable loss.
questions.q_fr: En 1911, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes refroidit du mercure à 4,2 degrés au-dessus du zéro absolu. Qu'est devenue sa résistance électrique ?
options_fr: Elle est restée exactement la même
questions.fact_fr: Un courant lancé dans une boucle supraconductrice continue de tourner sans pile et sans perte mesurable.

questions.why: All three numbers verified against Ring_of_Fire: 'About 90% of the world's earthquakes'; 'between 750 and 915 active or dormant volcanoes, around two-thirds of the world total'; approximately 40,000 km long, encircling the Pacific basin. Fact does not restate the question (it adds the volcano share and the length). Distractor oceans are same-kind and unambiguously wrong.
questions.q: The Ring of Fire, where about 90% of the world's earthquakes happen, runs around the edge of which ocean?
questions.fact: It also holds around two-thirds of the world's active volcanoes, strung along 40,000 km of colliding plate edges.
questions.q_fr: La ceinture de feu, où se produisent environ 90 % des séismes du globe, borde quel océan ?
questions.fact_fr: Elle réunit aussi environ deux tiers des volcans actifs du monde, le long de 40 000 km de bordures de plaques en collision.

questions.why: Correct: the missing mechanism was the central objection to continental drift. Distractor 0 is false because Wegener's fossil correlations (Mesosaurus, Glossopteris) were a pillar of his case, and distractor 2 is false because the coastline fit was his opening observation — so both are unambiguously wrong rather than partly defensible. The 1960s seafloor magnetic-stripe vindication is accurate and in the cited article. French idiomatic.
questions.q: In 1912 Alfred Wegener argued that the continents had once been joined and had since drifted apart. Why did most geologists reject the idea?
options: He had gathered no fossil evidence at all
He could not explain what force would move a continent
The coastlines plainly did not fit together
He never published the idea in his lifetime
questions.fact: Proof came from the seabed in the 1960s: stripes of magnetised rock beside mid-ocean ridges show new crust spreading outwards.
questions.q_fr: En 1912, Alfred Wegener soutint que les continents avaient été soudés puis s'étaient éloignés. Pourquoi la plupart des géologues rejetèrent-ils l'idée ?
options_fr: Il n'avait réuni aucune preuve fossile
Il n'expliquait pas quelle force pouvait déplacer un continent
Les côtes ne s'emboîtaient manifestement pas
Il n'a jamais publié son idée de son vivant
questions.fact_fr: La preuve est venue des fonds marins dans les années 1960 : des bandes de roche aimantée bordant les dorsales montrent la croûte qui s'écarte.

questions.why: English is clean: Wikipedia Marie_Tharp confirms the 1952 Mid-Atlantic rift valley discovery from sounding data and Bruce Heezen 'dismissing her explanation as girl talk'. Distractors are all real women in ocean/earth science — plausible, same kind, none of whom did this. The French was the problem: « paroles de fille » is not idiomatic French for 'girl talk' and reads as a mistranslation. Changed to « bavardages de fille » and restructured the sentence. Nothing else altered.
questions.q: Working from ship soundings in the 1950s, which scientist mapped a deep rift valley running down the middle of the Atlantic seafloor?
questions.fact: Her collaborator first dismissed the rift as 'girl talk'; it is in fact where new ocean floor is made.
questions.q_fr: À partir de sondages de navires, dans les années 1950, quelle scientifique cartographia une profonde vallée au milieu du fond de l'Atlantique ?
questions.fact_fr: Son collaborateur écarta d'abord sa découverte en la qualifiant de « bavardages de fille » ; c'est pourtant là que naît le plancher océanique.

questions.why: Answer and the dragon/toad mechanism verified against Zhang_Heng. The 132 CE date correctly disambiguates the seismoscope from his earlier armillary sphere, so distractor 0 is not a second right answer. But the fact said the ball dropped 'days before a messenger brought the news', while the article says only that 'a messenger arrived shortly afterwards' — 'days' is invented precision. Reworded, and swapped in the 400–500 km distance the article does give, which is a stronger payoff anyway. French updated.
questions.q: In 132 CE the Han-dynasty scholar Zhang Heng built a bronze instrument that could do what?
options: Predict eclipses a year in advance
Measure the height of distant mountains
Weigh a sealed container of air
Show the direction of a distant earthquake
questions.fact: Eight dragons held bronze balls; a tremor dropped one into a toad's mouth before any messenger could ride the 500 km with the news.
questions.q_fr: En 132, sous les Han, le savant Zhang Heng construisit un instrument de bronze capable de :
options_fr: prédire les éclipses un an à l'avance
mesurer la hauteur des montagnes lointaines
indiquer la direction d'un séisme lointain
questions.fact_fr: Huit dragons tenaient des billes de bronze ; une secousse en faisait tomber une dans la gueule d'un crapaud, avant qu'un messager ait pu faire les 500 km.

questions.why: Verified against 1883_eruption_of_Krakatoa: heard 4,800 km (3,000 mi) away at Rodrigues Island near Mauritius, where it was taken for 'cannon fire from a nearby ship'; barographs recorded the pressure wave rounding the globe three and a half times; 'the loudest sound that has ever been measured'. Distractor 1 (480 km) is the Perth-order decoy and 3,110 km to Perth is also real, so the 4,800 km option is correct and the others clearly short or absurd. Note: the kids:true flag is the weakest in the batch — a four-way numeric magnitude choice is a guess for a 10-year-old — but it is not a factual defect and the hook is strongly kid-facing, so I have left it.
questions.q: The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa, in what is now Indonesia, made what is thought to be the loudest sound in recorded history. How far away was it heard?
questions.fact: On Rodrigues Island, near Mauritius, it was mistaken for distant gunfire; barometers tracked the pressure wave circling the globe.
questions.q_fr: L'éruption du Krakatoa en 1883, dans l'actuelle Indonésie, produisit ce que l'on tient pour le son le plus fort jamais enregistré. À quelle distance l'a-t-on entendu ?
questions.fact_fr: Sur l'île Rodrigues, près de Maurice, on crut à des coups de canon lointains ; les baromètres suivirent l'onde faisant le tour du globe.

questions.why: Verified against Mount_Tambora: 'the largest in recorded history' (VEI 7, up to 150 km3 ejected), global cooling of 0.4–0.7 °C, June 1816 frosts and snow in New England, famine in Ireland, 'the worst famine of the 19th century'. So neither 'largest in recorded history' nor the failed-harvests claim is overstated. Distractors same-kind and plainly false.
questions.q: The eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia in 1815 was followed, half a world away, by what in 1816?
options: A 'year without a summer' and failed harvests
The draining of the Great Lakes
A complete halt to Atlantic storms
questions.fact: It was the largest eruption in recorded history: the ash cooled the whole planet and crops failed across the northern hemisphere.
questions.q_fr: L'éruption du mont Tambora, en Indonésie, en 1815 fut suivie en 1816, à l'autre bout du monde, par quoi ?
options_fr: Une « année sans été » et des récoltes perdues
questions.fact_fr: C'est la plus forte éruption jamais enregistrée : les cendres ont refroidi toute la planète et les récoltes ont manqué dans l'hémisphère nord.

questions.why: Stratosphere is correct and the other three are the real neighbouring layers — good same-kind distractors with no second defensible answer. The Montreal Protocol (1987) and the slow recovery of the Antarctic ozone hole are both in the cited article and 'slowly closing' is appropriately hedged rather than declaring the problem solved. kids:true is marginal for a four-way layer-name discrimination but defensible at diff 2.
questions.q: Which layer of the atmosphere holds the ozone that absorbs most of the Sun's ultraviolet light?
questions.fact: The 1987 Montreal Protocol phased out the chemicals thinning it, and the Antarctic ozone hole is slowly closing.
questions.q_fr: Quelle couche de l'atmosphère contient l'ozone qui absorbe l'essentiel des ultraviolets solaires ?
questions.fact_fr: Le protocole de Montréal de 1987 a supprimé les produits qui l'attaquaient, et le trou d'ozone antarctique se referme lentement.

questions.why: Answer correct and confirmed. But the fact overstated frequency: it said north and south 'often' light up as mirror images, whereas Wikipedia files conjugate auroras under 'Abnormal types' and says they 'generally happen at the time of the equinoxes, when there is little difference in the orientation of the north and south geomagnetic poles to the Sun'. Downgraded 'often' to 'can' and added the equinox condition, which also makes the fact more interesting. French rewritten to match.
questions.q: What creates the aurora — the northern and southern lights?
options: Sunlight bouncing off the polar ice and back into the sky
Charged particles from the Sun striking gases high above us
Lightning storms flashing inside very high clouds
Moonlight scattered by ice crystals in the upper air
questions.fact: North and south can light up as near mirror images at the same moment, on the same magnetic field lines — usually near the equinoxes.
questions.q_fr: Qu'est-ce qui crée les aurores polaires ?
options_fr: La lumière du Soleil réfléchie par la glace polaire vers le ciel
Des particules chargées venues du Soleil qui frappent les gaz en altitude
Des orages qui éclatent à l'intérieur de nuages très élevés
Le clair de lune diffusé par les cristaux de glace en altitude
questions.fact_fr: Les deux pôles peuvent s'illuminer en quasi-miroir au même instant, sur les mêmes lignes de champ magnétique — surtout près des équinoxes.

questions.why: Correct: the name comes from fishermen off the coast of Peru, referring to the Christ Child because the warming appears around Christmas. Distractors are all countries with a real Pacific or maritime connection (Japan, Australia) or a Spanish/Portuguese-language decoy (Portugal), so they are plausible without being defensible. Fact is not a restatement — it supplies the meaning of the name.
questions.q: El Niño, the warm Pacific event that shifts weather worldwide, was named by fishermen of which country?
questions.fact: They called the warm current 'the Christ Child' because it showed up around Christmas.
questions.q_fr: El Niño, le réchauffement du Pacifique qui bouleverse le climat mondial, fut nommé par les pêcheurs de quel pays ?
questions.fact_fr: Ils appelaient ce courant chaud « l'Enfant Jésus » parce qu'il se manifestait aux alentours de Noël.

questions.why: Verified against Milutin_Milankovic: he 'considered three cyclical movements of the Earth: eccentricity, axial tilt, and precession'; arrested by Austro-Hungarian authorities in 1914, sent to a camp at Nezsider, then released to Budapest where the Director of the Library of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences 'enabled him to work undisturbed' for nearly the whole war. 'Interned in Budapest during the First World War' is accurate. Distractors are strong: Agassiz established ice ages and Wegener collaborated with Milankovic — plausible, same kind, neither derived the cycles.
questions.q: Ice ages come and go with slow changes in Earth's orbit and tilt. Which scientist worked out the cycles behind them?
questions.fact: He did much of the mathematics by hand while interned in Budapest during the First World War.
questions.q_fr: Les glaciations vont et viennent au rythme de lentes variations de l'orbite et de l'inclinaison de la Terre. Quel scientifique en a calculé les cycles ?
questions.fact_fr: Il réalisa une grande partie des calculs à la main pendant son internement à Budapest, durant la Première Guerre mondiale.

questions.why: Verified against Tidal_locking: synchronous rotation, orbital period matching rotational period, and 'about 59 percent of the Moon's total surface may be seen with repeated observations from Earth, due to the phenomena of libration and parallax'. The 59% figure and the elliptical/tilted-orbit explanation are both in the article. Distractor 0 ('it does not rotate at all') is the classic misconception and is genuinely wrong. French preserves order.
questions.q: Why do we always see the same face of the Moon from Earth?
options: It does not rotate at all
It turns once on its axis for every orbit it makes
It is not really a sphere
Earth's shadow hides the far side
questions.fact: Its orbit is slightly oval and tilted, so over time we glimpse about 59% of the surface, not just half.
questions.q_fr: Pourquoi voit-on toujours la même face de la Lune depuis la Terre ?
options_fr: Elle ne tourne pas du tout sur elle-même
Elle fait un tour sur elle-même à chaque orbite
L'ombre de la Terre cache la face cachée
questions.fact_fr: Son orbite est légèrement ovale et inclinée : avec le temps, on aperçoit environ 59 % de sa surface, et non la moitié.

questions.why: Slug verified as a live article titled exactly 'Lunar Laser Ranging experiments'. It confirms retroreflectors from Apollo 11, 14 and 15 plus Lunokhod 1 and 2 (and now Chandrayaan-3), and states 'The Moon is spiraling away from Earth at a rate of 3.8 cm/year'. The fingernail-growth comparison is a fair everyday analogue (~3.5 cm/yr). Question stem correctly credits both American and Soviet hardware.
questions.q: Apollo astronauts and Soviet rovers left mirrors on the Moon. What are scientists on Earth still doing with them?
options: Reflecting sunlight to light up future landing sites
Sending coded signals onward to other spacecraft
Bouncing laser beams off them to measure the Moon's distance
Watching for the flashes of meteorite impacts
questions.fact: The measurements show the Moon drifting about 3.8 cm farther away each year — roughly the rate fingernails grow.
questions.q_fr: Les astronautes d'Apollo et des engins soviétiques ont laissé des miroirs sur la Lune. À quoi servent-ils encore aujourd'hui ?
options_fr: À réfléchir le Soleil pour éclairer de futurs sites d'atterrissage
À relayer des signaux codés vers d'autres engins spatiaux
À y renvoyer des faisceaux laser pour mesurer la distance de la Lune
À guetter les éclairs des impacts de météorites
questions.fact_fr: Ces mesures montrent que la Lune s'éloigne d'environ 3,8 cm par an — à peu près la vitesse de pousse des ongles.

questions.why: The 650-million-to-1.4-billion-year range was the item I most expected to be invented; it is quoted verbatim in Solar_eclipse: 'Estimates of the time when the Moon will be unable to occlude the entire Sun when viewed from Earth range between 650 million and 1.4 billion years in the future.' The 400x/400x coincidence is correct. Distractor 0 inverts the actual relationship and is unambiguously false. The correct option is slightly the most specific, but options 1 and 3 are comparable in length so the giveaway is minor.
questions.q: A total solar eclipse is only possible thanks to a coincidence. What is it?
options: The Moon and the Sun are almost exactly the same true size
The Moon's orbit around Earth happens to be a perfect circle
The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, and 400 times farther
Earth and the Moon happen to spin at exactly the same rate
questions.fact: Because the Moon is slowly moving away, total eclipses will stop between 650 million and 1.4 billion years from now.
questions.q_fr: Une éclipse totale de Soleil n'est possible que grâce à une coïncidence. Laquelle ?
options_fr: La Lune et le Soleil ont presque exactement la même taille réelle
L'orbite de la Lune autour de la Terre est un cercle parfait
Le Soleil est environ 400 fois plus large que la Lune, et 400 fois plus loin
La Terre et la Lune tournent exactement à la même vitesse
questions.fact_fr: Comme la Lune s'éloigne lentement, les éclipses totales cesseront dans 650 millions à 1,4 milliard d'années.

questions.why: Answer correct, but the sourcing failed. The pulsar payoff — the single best part of the item — is NOT in SN_1054, which mentions the Crab Pulsar without any spin rate or size. I moved src to Crab_Nebula, which is the article about the answer, carries a photograph, links the nebula to the 1054 guest star recorded by Chinese astronomers, and states 'a neutron star 28–30 kilometres across with a spin rate of 30.2 times per second'. Because Crab_Nebula gives daytime visibility but not the 23-day duration, I removed '23 days' from the stem so every claim is checkable in the cited article. French updated identically.
questions.q: In 1054 Chinese astronomers logged a 'guest star' bright enough to be seen in broad daylight. What do we call its remains today?
questions.fact: At its centre spins a pulsar: a star barely 30 km across, turning about 30 times every second.
questions.q_fr: En 1054, des astronomes chinois notèrent une « étoile invitée » visible en plein jour. Comment appelle-t-on ses restes aujourd'hui ?
questions.fact_fr: En son centre tourne un pulsar : une étoile d'à peine 30 km de diamètre, qui fait environ 30 tours par seconde.

questions.why: Slug fetched and live. Abd_al-Rahman_al-Sufi confirms 'the earliest recorded observation of the Andromeda Galaxy in 964, describing it as a small cloud' and that it 'was the first galaxy other than the Milky Way to be mentioned in writing' — so the fact is not overstated. Book of Fixed Stars completed 964. Telescope 1608, so 'more than six centuries before' is right. Centres a Persian astronomer on his own terms.
questions.q: In 964 the Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi described a 'small cloud' in the night sky. What was it?
questions.fact: It is the first galaxy beyond our own ever written down — more than six centuries before the telescope existed.
questions.q_fr: En 964, l'astronome persan Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi décrivit un « petit nuage » dans le ciel nocturne. De quoi s'agissait-il ?
questions.fact_fr: C'est la première galaxie autre que la nôtre jamais consignée par écrit — plus de six siècles avant l'invention de la lunette.

questions.why: Answer confirmed: the Emu in the Sky 'consists of dark nebulae ... visible against the Milky Way background', head being the Coalsack. The egg-harvest timing is also confirmed — 'When the constellation is close to the horizon as the sun is setting, the people know that it is the right time to harvest emu eggs' — but the article attributes this specifically to the Yamatji, and the generic 'a calendar written in the dark patches of the sky' flattened that. Named the people, per the Perspective Rubric. French rewritten.
questions.q: Many Aboriginal Australian peoples see an emu in the night sky. What is that constellation made of?
options: An alignment of seven especially bright stars
Dark dust clouds silhouetted against the Milky Way
A tight cluster of unusually red giant stars
The glowing trail left behind by a bright comet
questions.fact: For the Yamatji, when the emu sits low on the horizon at sunset it is time to harvest emu eggs — a calendar in the sky's dark patches.
questions.q_fr: De nombreux peuples aborigènes d'Australie voient un émeu dans le ciel nocturne. De quoi cette constellation est-elle faite ?
options_fr: D'un alignement de sept étoiles particulièrement brillantes
De nuages de poussière sombres se détachant sur la Voie lactée
D'un amas serré d'étoiles géantes rouges
De la traînée lumineuse laissée par une comète
questions.fact_fr: Chez les Yamatji, quand l'émeu est bas sur l'horizon au coucher du soleil, c'est le moment de récolter les œufs : un calendrier inscrit dans les zones sombres du ciel.

questions.why: Every figure verified against Jantar_Mantar,_Jaipur: 'The monument was completed in 1734'; the Vrihat Samrat Yantra is the world's largest stone sundial at 88 feet (27 m); its shadow moves 'visibly at 1 mm per second, or roughly a hand's breadth (6 cm) every minute'. Distractors are all real historic astronomical instruments, none of which this is. Centres the Jaipur observatory on its own terms with its own name.
questions.q: The Vrihat Samrat Yantra, completed at Jaipur in India in 1734, is the world's largest stone example of which instrument?
questions.fact: Its 27-metre gnomon casts a shadow that creeps about a millimetre a second: you can stand there and watch time move.
questions.q_fr: Le Vrihat Samrat Yantra, achevé à Jaipur en Inde en 1734, est le plus grand exemplaire en pierre de quel instrument ?
questions.fact_fr: Son gnomon de 27 mètres projette une ombre qui avance d'environ un millimètre par seconde : on voit littéralement le temps passer.

questions.why: Answer correct. Two accuracy problems in the fact. First, the cited Chicxulub_crater article gives the diameter as 'two hundred kilometers (120 mi)', not 180 km — the 180 figure is an older estimate and would not check out against the source. Second, Penfield and Camargo were geophysicists, not geologists, per the same article ('geophysicists who had been looking for petroleum ... working for ... Pemex'). Both corrected; the pleasing 'not fossil hunters but oil prospectors' twist is preserved. French updated.
questions.q: The crater left by the asteroid impact linked to the extinction of the dinosaurs lies buried beneath which region?
questions.fact: About 200 km across, it was found not by fossil hunters but by geophysicists surveying the ground for oil.
questions.q_fr: Le cratère laissé par l'astéroïde associé à l'extinction des dinosaures est enfoui sous quelle région ?
options_fr: La péninsule du Yucatán, au Mexique
questions.fact_fr: Large d'environ 200 km, il a été repéré non par des paléontologues mais par des géophysiciens en prospection pétrolière.

questions.why: Voyager_1 confirms launch 5 September 1977 and 'crossed the heliopause and entered interstellar space on August 25, 2012, making it the first spacecraft to do so'. The Golden Record contents check out on the linked article: 'spoken greetings in 55 ancient and modern languages', whale sounds and music, on a gold-plated copper disc. Pioneer 10 is a genuinely strong distractor (launched earlier, once expected to lead) but was overtaken and is not in interstellar space; Cassini and New Horizons are wrong on both counts.
questions.q: Which spacecraft, launched in 1977, became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space?
questions.fact: It carries a gold-plated record of greetings in 55 languages, whale song and music, in case anyone ever finds it.
questions.q_fr: Quel engin spatial, lancé en 1977, est devenu le premier objet humain à atteindre l'espace interstellaire ?
questions.fact_fr: Il emporte un disque plaqué or avec des salutations en 55 langues, des chants de baleines et de la musique, au cas où on le trouverait.

questions.why: All four claims verified against Chandrayaan-3: landing 23 August 2023 at 69°S; 'the first in human history to achieve a soft landing near the lunar south pole'; 'ISRO became the fourth national space agency to successfully land on the Moon'; and the Pragyan rover's LIBS instrument 'unambiguously confirmed the presence of sulfur in the lunar surface near the south pole'. Distractors are apt: Japan (SLIM) and Israel (Beresheet) both attempted lunar landings, so they are plausible without being right.
questions.q: In August 2023, which country's mission made the first soft landing near the Moon's south pole?
questions.fact: Its rover Pragyan found sulphur in the soil, and India became the fourth nation to land softly on the Moon.
questions.q_fr: En août 2023, la mission de quel pays a réussi le premier alunissage en douceur près du pôle sud lunaire ?
questions.fact_fr: Son rover Pragyan a détecté du soufre dans le sol, et l'Inde est devenue le quatrième pays à se poser en douceur sur la Lune.
